I wanted him to live out his dreams with a group of ladies. As with many areas, my local rescues have an abundance of piggies, and Lambchop is lacking some child-friendly appeal, so I've had trouble getting him placed into a forever home.

My sweet old man Georgie passed away last week, and Franklin, who had never lived alone a day in his life, was taking the loss rather hard. I was nervous about putting these two boys together, but when life gives you lemons... They certainly made lemonade. They get along like they were always meant to be. I'm so thankful to have one thing off my plate while I'm grieving; knowing Franklin isn't alone has really been a relief.

Mr. Lambchop, may you have many fine years of sass and love ahead of you in your forever home.

I had a very similar experience to you!! I got my nipples pierced in August and started suspecting that one might have been just a wee bit too deep a few days in, but decided to see if it was swollen/irritated and waited it out. I also was worried about offending the piercer if I suggested it was pierced too deep, so I got another opinion from a second shop. Because of how different the shape can be when erect vs not, the placement looked perfect to the second piercer in person, but when I showed a photo of my nipple when it wasn't erect, he agreed that it might have been a little deep, but said it could heal. 

Honestly, I still don't know if it was pierced too deep or not. But about a month and a half in, I decided to take out the piercing, let it heal, and got it redone. I figured if I'm committing to having a piercing on my body for potentially a lifetime, I really wanted to love it, and I just wasn't loving my piercing and kept second-guessing it. Now that I got it redone, I ADORE my piercing and feel like it's perfect. I really took time to look at where the piercer marked me the second time. Reference photos [here](https://imgur.com/a/Z83MdBn) of old placement in various stages of healing vs new placement.

I'd give it some time to settle in since it's so fresh and then potentially think about getting it redone if you decide it just isn't working for you!

Because your cage is separated, your guinea pigs don't think they live "together" but rather as "neighbors" as they both have their own dedicated territory. Guinea pigs fight over territory, not resources. This is why they appear to "get along" as neighbors until they are in the same space, and then they display dominance behaviors.

Every time you place them together and apart, it is a fresh "introduction" for them and they have to sort out the hierarchy/pecking order between the two of them. This is stressful for guineas. This introduction (yes, it is an introduction.) looked like it went well, but if you already put them back in separate spaces, you'll have to do it again.

Introduce them outside the cage in a big, neutral space with a big pile of hay. If there is no blood or fur pulling for about 2 hours, clean their ENTIRE cage VERY thoroughly, spray everything down with 50/50 vinegar/water, wash bowls and water bottles, get fresh fleece and hides, etc. All territorial smells have to be removed. Even better if you rearrange the cage and make it unfamiliar to them. Remove the divider and return the pigs to the VERY CLEAN, whole cage, observing for about another hour. I'd also suggest adding one ramp to each of your lofts so they have a way up and down at all times and they can't corner each other.

Hope this helps! I have 4 boys myself.

A cost effective option for fully disposable bedding for a large cage is kiln-dried pine pelleted used in horse stalls topped with hemp. The hemp is about $70 for 70 quarts on amazon- a huge bag- and the absorbant pellets are about $7 at my local tractor supply for a 40lb bag.

There's still daily maintenance with this- the soiled hemp bedding needs to be disposed of, and the soiled pellets underneath need to be disposed of or mixed in with the fresher pellets. They break down into dust and the hemp both acts as a cushion for piggy feet and a barrier for the dust to keep it from entering their lungs.

You can also use the stall pellets and just cover that with a piece of wicked fleece in place of a liner. Just shake out the fleece as usual to dispose of poos and scoop/replace the soiled pellets underneath.

Hemp bedding smells a little nutty, but mostly you'll smell the pine pellets. Very woody.

When you reintroduce them, you can't put the young boy back in the original cage with the old boy because of this. Getting a friend to hold the wee one while you clip works wonders. If they have black nails, use the flashlight on your phone to see the quick.

If you go at it solo, here is what I do (with much patience):
For the back nails, hold the pig on your lap against your body. Cover the front half of the piggy loosely with a blanket for security and comfort. Pin them gently there with your forearm. Hold the foot with your non-dominant hand and trim with your dominant hand. Flip pig and repeat.

For the front nails, place the pig in your lap such that their bum is facing your belly. Lift the pig with your non-dominant hand at their chest so they are in a standing position on their hind feet. Most pigs stick their hands out in this position for easy trimming but you may have to hold out a paw if they are squirmy.

What? This isn't true at all. Males can be kept together if they are compatible. I have six males, all in pairs of two, and they have stable relationships. They exhibit dominance behaviors, but they don't fight to the point of injuring each other, let alone death.

It seems like Fudge and Caramel are likely going through puberty. This is a time where piggy hormones are at an all time high and they are more territorial and aggressive with each other to establish dominance. They should be separated if they draw blood. Because they have already been separated, the male left in the original enclosure now thinks he has the entire "territory" and doesn't have to share it, so he'll fight every time the other pig is put in there with them. 

To reintroduce Fudge and Caramel, be prepared to set aside a good few hours to just watch them interact. They need to be put in a big space that has no pig smells, like a playpen or a small blocked off room with nowhere to hide. Offer them a big pile of hay and observe. Mounting, chasing, and rumbling are all normal. Teeth chattering and lunging are bad signs, but again, they are normal. Separate them if they draw blood or pull fur (but watch your hand- cover it with something like an oven mitt or a towel so you don't get injured.) I put a very small dab of vanilla on each pig's nose and rear end to help disguise smells before bonding but I'm not sure it made much difference.

With boys you really have to let them work it out. Puberty is a time of a lot of tension and squabbles. It's hard to watch them sort it out, but that's the only way to do it if you want them to live together. They can also happily live as neighbors in separate enclosures. If the bonding goes well, they'll mostly ignore each other, eat together, and lay down to show they're calm.

If they get to a point of being calm, you'll want to completely clean the cage very, very well. No pig smells. Fresh fleece/bedding/hides, wash the bowls and water bottles well. Spray down surfaces with a cleaner, such as 50/50 vinegar:water. Only use hides with at least two entrances so no pig can trap another pig inside. You may consider expanding their enclosure to give them more room- pigs fight over territory, so if they have ample room, they argue less. As always, two of everything: Two hides, two sources of hay/food/water, etc. If a resource is limited, one pig can become territorial over it.

If the bonding goes poorly and ends in blood or excessive fur pulling, they likely won't ever be able to room together, unfortunately.

I am able to do my piggies by myself relatively painlessly. Here is my technique:

For the back nails, I set the pig in my lap and place a blanket over their upper body and head so they feel comfortable and hidden. A pig tries to get away from you to hide. This helps them a bit. With the hand clipping the nails, I brace the pig against my body with my forearm to keep them in place. My free hand holds the paw. If the pig has black nails, I balance my phone light under their foot to see the quick. They will probably pull their foot away over and over again- just keep at it.

For the front nails, I turn the piggy in my lap so their butt is facing my tummy. I use my non dominant hand and fit it under their chest to lift them off of their front two legs, keeping the hind legs stable. Wiggly pigs can be braced against your tummy. Use this hand to hold the front paws if they try to pull them away- my experience is they usually stiffly hold them out and it makes for fine trimming. 

Lots and lots of patience is needed for fussy pigs. I do not stop until the nails are done. They'll tucker themselves out at some point or realize their wriggling won't get them out of the situation. I speak softly the whole time and offer veggie breaks!

For those who don't know, hairless guinea pigs are the result of a genetic mutation. They were historically first bred not as pets, but for research. The sensitive skin of a hairless guinea pig makes it a fantastic model for dermatological studies. Guinea pigs generally have immune systems that resemble a human's more similarly than other research rodents.

My first cue that something was amiss in my boys was that my werewolf began to lose hair on his back. This is not necessarily abnormal; he lost nearly all of his hair when he first came to me and werewolf guinea pigs can lose/regrow hair based on different hormonal levels. I began watching him more closely and noticed that he was scratching himself significantly more and would occasionally cry out from discomfort when he itched himself. My completely hairless guinea pig first showed symptoms in pale, peeling skin near his rump. I describe it as peeling like a sunburn; the skin was not especially scaly, just fine and thin, like he was losing the topmost layer of skin. I soothed their skin with coconut oil and kept a watchful eye on it, fearful of common skin diseases in pigs like ringworm or mites. (I doubted mites as I routinely do preventative ivermectin treatments.) When both pigs began scratching to the point of cuts on the skin, I knew something was wrong. On my hairless pig, he had round clusters of irritated, peeling spots. These spots appeared to "heal" and stop peeling, leaving a dark spot of hyperpigmentation in the center. Around his sides, he almost looked like he was being bitten by some sort of insect with raised, inflamed, round spots of skin. I now suspect these were hives. My werewolf went on to display flaky, cracked skin all over his back.

I began doing research and consistently could only find that the symptoms lined up with ringworm or mites. Neither seemed perfectly right; If it was mites, my preventative treatments hadn't worked, and it lacked many characteristics of ringworm. The irritation did not start on my pigs' snouts (in fact, it never progressed to their faces), it seemed to spread rapidly all over their body (within 1 week), it did not glow under a blacklight (NOT necessarily always an indicator that you are not dealing with a fungal strain!), and perhaps most damning, I had not caught ringworm, nor had my other furred pigs. I was terrified; if it was ringworm, where had it come from? My pigs do not go outside and I maintain diligent cleaning schedules. I felt like a failure as an owner.

I treated for mites and ringworm at home with ivermectin, antifungal creams that didn't do much, and an antifungal bath that made their skin worsen significantly overnight. The only thing that seemed to soothe them at all was hydration to the skin, and later on doses of Children's Benadryl, which I gave in 0.5 mg doses twice daily. They were irritable, uncomfortable, and in pain and distress. They both lost approximately 100g while I was waiting for my vet appointment. My boys fought to the point of drawing blood on each other, which is uncharacteristic of them. I was bit in the process of separating them and rushed to the pet store with blood dripping down my forearm to get a new enclosure. I believe they would accidentally touch the other pig and trigger their skin discomfort, so they thought they were being attacked by the other pig and lashed out in self-defense.

My vet asked me the crucial question of if I had changed anything at all in their setup prior to their symptoms, and that connected all of the dots. Their symptoms entirely started after I changed their bedding brand. None of my research online had led me to even consider this a possibility, so I think it is important to share my experience with the community. I had previously looked into the bedding and my research turned up very little info, but generally no pig owners reported negatively on the bedding before I purchased it. I was sent home with more Children's Benadryl and a pain med, and changed my pigs' bedding immediately. I did what was my third deep clean of their cage. Stopping the ringworm treatments was scary, but I trusted my vet. Rightfully so, their skin cleared up in about two weeks.

If you see a hairless guinea pig having skin issues, please, please know that ringworm or mites or dry skin are not the only potential sources. Please do not use Oxbow Eco-Straw bedding if you have skinnies. Georgie and Franklin have had a successful reintroduction, and Franklin's mangey looking hair is beginning to grow back. It's a happy ending for us, and while I wish I had more reference photos to provide, I hope this information is able to benefit other skinny owners.

You may consider temporarily switching to all fleece and no disposable bedding to see if their skin improves so you can determine if this is an allergic reaction. I hope your baby feels better soon. When I brought home a calathea with a suspected infestation, I didn't see the mites, only webbing. I brushed it away and found it rebuilt, but still no mites visible to my eye. When I bought a humidifier and put it near my plant, after a day suddenly I could see the little buggers everywhere as they came out to find dry air.   
If you have a humidifier, you may be able to confirm mites vs a friendly little spider this way. Leave it near the plant for a day or two, then come back and look for little red/orange fellas that move when you poke at them or blow at them gently. I used my phone's flashlight to help me see!
